review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The retinoblastoma protein (RB) is a well-characterized repressor of E2F
transcriptional activity that controls genes involved in cell proliferation during the G1 phase.
Here, we examine the effect of RB on chromatin organization and uncover a non-canonical role
for RB in which it promotes the removal of cohesin from insulators and thereby induces the
expression of adjacent genes. We identify that RB colocalizes with cohesin across the human
genome. During mitosis, RB facilitates the removal of cohesin from CTCF sites, with this effect
persisting into early G1, impacting loop formation and extrusion at topologically associating
domain (TAD) boundaries. Chromosome conformation capture assays reveal that RB reduces
insulation at TAD boundaries and promotes enhancer-promoter interactions marked by histone 3
lysine 27 acetylation. In this way, RB enhances the transcription of hundreds of genes beyond
the E2F transcriptional program, a finding that expands our understanding of this key tumor
suppressor and cell cycle regulator.

---

## Introduction

The retinoblastoma gene RB1 was the first tumor suppressor to be molecularly defined and is often
described as a prototypical tumor suppressor1,2. Its protein product, RB, is a critical cell cycle regulator
that represses the transcriptional program required for cell proliferation. Active RB associates with E2F-
regulated promoters and represses the transcription of cell cycle genes, preventing cell cycle
advancement1. Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity phosphorylates RB, inhibiting its association with
E2F3-6 and promoting E2F-dependent transcription and cell cycle progression2,7,8.

RB1 is genetically or functionally inactivated in most types of cancer9,10. More frequently, cancer
cells acquire mutations that increase cyclin D-CDK4/6 or cyclin E-CDK2 kinase activity, leading to
hyper-phosphorylation and functional inactivation of RB10. However, some cancers can directly target RB
through loss-of-function mutations and loss of heterozygosity in the RB1 gene itself11-13. RB1 mutations
are often late events during tumor evolution14,15, and RB-deficient tumors exhibit unique characteristics
that are not fully explained by the RB/E2F model and its role in the regulation of cell proliferation16.
These include the histological trans-differentiation of adenocarcinoma to neuroendocrine tumors and the
development of acquired resistance to targeted therapies14,15,17-19, increased genomic instability associated
with compromised sister chromatid cohesion20-22, and heightened metastatic potential in lung and prostate
cancers14,15,19. These non-canonical roles of RB raise the question of whether it might have additional
functions in transcriptional regulation beyond the direct inhibition of E2F-targeted genes.

Recently, we discovered that RB’s association with E2F-bound promoters represents only a portion of
the chromatin-bound population of RB23. RB is also associated with AP-1-bound enhancers and CTCF
insulators23, which may suggest an emerging model in which RB regulates transcription by interacting
with different types of cis-regulatory elements. Fluctuations in RB phosphorylation at CDK sites control
RB distribution between promoters and enhancers but have less influence on RB’s association with
insulators23,24. Microscopic studies, including our own, have revealed that RB plays an important role in
regulating nuclear morphology25,26. Since CTCF sites are the primary anchors for the cell’s loop extrusion
machinery27-30, which regulates transcription partly through chromatin insulation31-33, and since RB’s
association with CTCF sites is mostly cell cycle-independent and conserved across cell types23,34, we
hypothesized that RB might exert non-canonical transcriptional regulation by modulating DNA loops.

Here, by employing chromosome conformation capture with nucleosome resolution35, we reveal that
RB is an essential regulator of cohesin-dependent loops at CTCF insulators. Loss of RB increased the
number and size of DNA loops and the stability of topologically associating domains (TADs). We
observed that RB and cohesin were associated genome-wide at accessible chromatin regions. In RB-
deficient cells, cohesin was less effectively removed from CTCF insulators, resulting in its accumulation
and enhanced insulation. Cell cycle synchronization experiments showed that the RB-mediated
deregulation of cohesin distribution peaked during mitosis and persisted into early G1. The enhanced
insulation at CTCF sites following RB loss diminished enhancer-promoter interactions assessed by
histone 3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) HiChIP36. Overall, we demonstrate that by facilitating
cohesin removal from insulators and promoting enhancer-promoter interactions, RB activates hundreds of
genes outside of the E2F transcriptional program.

---

## Results

RB is a regulator of chromatin organization
To characterize the impact of RB in chromatin organization, we employed Micro-C35, a chromosome
conformation capture method with nucleosome resolution. We conducted two complementary sets of
experiments in human retinal pigment epithelial cells immortalized by telomerase reverse transcriptase
(hTERT-RPE1) (Figs. 1a and b) to compare the effects of (1) conditional gain of constitutively active RB
and (2) chronic RB deficiency. Cell cycle synchronization was used to minimize potential confounding
variables between the two experimental systems. In the first set of experiments, we studied the role of
unphosphorylated RB, which has been described to trigger visible changes in nuclear architecture and
promote chromatin dispersion25. To examine these microscopic findings in chromosome conformation
capture, we utilized the same cellular model, replacing the endogenous RB with a constitutively active
FLAG-tagged variant (RBΔCDK) via a doxycycline-inducible system23,25,37. The RBΔCDK variant harbors 14
missense mutations that substitute all known endogenous CDK phosphorylation sites with alanine37,38.
Following 24 h of doxycycline treatment, cells entered the G0/G1 phase, and upon 72 h, they exited the
cell cycle and developed a chromatin dispersion phenotype25. In the second set of experiments, we aimed
to distinguish RB’s role in chromatin organization from changes related to cell cycle. To model RB loss,
we utilized RB1 knockout hTERT-RPE1 cells generated with the CRISPR/Cas9 system (Supplementary
Fig. 1)39. These cells were synchronized in G1 phase via 6 days of contact inhibition and then
subsequently released to S phase via trypsinization (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 2).

Chromosome conformation capture recapitulated many of the expected features of chromatin
organization, including chromosome territories40, nuclear compartments41, topologically associating
domains (TADs)42,43, cohesin-dependent loops27,44, and architectural stripes45 (Fig. 1a, Supplementary
Figs. 3 and 4). To identify the overall scale at which RB-dependent changes in chromatin organization
occur, we measured the contact probability (P(s)), which assesses the likelihood of contact formation as a
function of genomic separation (Fig. 1c)44,46. The contact probability curve has been shown to have at
least two different regimes in mammalian cells, among which a shallow decay for s < 200 kb has been
reported to be produced by cohesin-dependent loop formation44,47. In our chromosome conformation
capture, we identified three major regimes in the contact probability curve: the cohesin-dependent decay
for s < 200 kb (P(s) ≈ s-0.8), a steeper decay for 200 kb < s < 3 Mb (P(s) ≈ s-1.3), and a variable far-cis
scaling for s > 3Mb (Fig. 1c).

Expression of RB∆CDK caused significant changes in chromatin structures at s > 3 Mb, often
associated with far-cis contacts between nuclear compartments44,47. Accordingly, when RB∆CDK was
expressed, the most striking change in chromatin organization occurred in the distribution of nuclear
compartments and their interactions (Fig. 1d). Nuclear compartments are chromatin features that are
thought to be cohesin-independent44. Although changes that occurred between 0h and 24h or 72h of
RB∆CDK expression may be associated with G1-arrest, most compartmental changes occurred between 24
h and 72 h of RB∆CDK expression, coinciding with the irreversible cell cycle exit, as previously
described25. We observed the spreading of compartment B to adjacent regions and increased spatial
distance within compartment B (Fig. 1d), concordant with the previously described heterochromatin
dispersion phenotype (Fig. 1e)25.

In contrast, the loss of RB in G1-synchronized cells affected chromatin interaction at s < 200 kb and
200 kb < s < 3 Mb (Fig. 1c). In both regimes, RB loss led to steeper decays, shifting the contact probability
curves to P(s) ≈ s-0.85 (s < 200 kb) and P(s) ≈ s-1.35 (200 kb < s < 3 Mb). The steeper decay at the cohesin-
dependent regime for s < 200 kb suggested that RB may regulate cohesin-dependent loop formation
independently from its effect on cell cycle. Indeed, in cells synchronized in the G1 phase, RB loss increased
the number of cohesin-dependent loops by 40.5% (Fig. 1f; p-value = 3.66×10-7, two-tailed paired Student’s
t-test) and increased the average size of these loops by 16.4 kb (Fig. 1g; p-value = 1.86×10-2, two-tailed
Student’s t-test). In RB-depleted cells, these loops also produced stronger domains, as evidenced by
increased TAD strength in RBKO compared to RBWT (Fig. 1h). These changes were not observed in cells
accumulated in S phase (Figs. 1f and g). Furthermore, three-dimensional reconstruction of the chromatin
architecture, via a cell population-based algorithm, revealed that RB loss weakens the spatial clustering of
acrocentric chromosomes harboring nucleolus organizer regions (NORs). Specifically, the average distance
between centromeres of acrocentric chromosomes grew from ~1.81 µm in RBWT to ~2.52 µm in RBKO
(Supplementary Figs. 5–7). This Micro-C data corroborated previous microscopic observations26,
positioning RB as a significant regulator of the cohesin-dependent interphase chromatin architecture. In
summary, we observe that RB exerts broad effects on chromatin organization (Fig. 1i), with RB∆CDK
expression promoting primarily heterochromatin spreading and dispersion (Figs. 1d–e), and RB loss in G1-
arrested cells altering cohesin-dependent loop number, loop length, and TAD boundary strength (Figs. 1g–
h).

Genome-wide association of RB and cohesin
Given that the loss of RB promoted cohesin-dependent loop formation, we assessed whether
chromatin-bound RB is associated with genomic loci bound by cohesin. For this, we performed chromatin
immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) for SMC3 in hTERT-RPE1 cells. We also performed ChIP-
seq experiments for various histone modifications to annotate active promoters and enhancers (H3K4me3,
H3K4me1, H3K27ac) and heterochromatin (H3K27me3) and for transcription factors previously reported
to colocalize with RB at cis-regulatory elements (E2F1, CTCF, and c-Jun)23. To assess chromatin
accessibility at these loci, we performed assays for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing
(ATAC-seq).

Strikingly, RB showed extensive colocalization with SMC3 in the human genome (Figs. 2a and b):
68.7% of RB binding sites exhibited SMC3 binding as well (Fig. 2a). This overlap was strongest at
insulators, where 99.6% of RB binding sites showed SMC3 binding. Notably, the overlap between RB
and SMC3 was significantly more extensive than that between RB and E2F1, which was only evident in
promoter regions. Besides the association with SMC3, all chromatin regions bound by RB were highly
accessible (Fig. 2b).

Cohesin is a loop extrusion machinery that utilizes energy from ATP hydrolysis to form chromatin
loops28,29. We wondered, therefore, if RB binding sites also demonstrate insulation of chromatin contacts
at a comparable level to that observed at cohesin binding sites. To quantify the strength of insulation,
we measured the insulation score from chromosome conformation capture, with more negative values
indicating stronger insulation48,49. Indeed, RB binding sites were significantly more insulating compared
to the genome-wide average (Fig. 2c; p-value < 0.0001, two-tailed Student’s t-test), and were comparable
to the insulation strength at SMC3 binding sites. At CTCF binding sites, which showed the strongest
insulation on average (Fig. 2c; p-value < 0.0001, two-tailed Student’s t-test), the co-occurrence of RB
binding further increased insulation (Fig. 2c; p-value < 0.0001, two-tailed Student’s t-test). Notably, RB-
bound CTCF sites were significantly more accessible compared to non-RB-bound CTCF sites (Fig. 2d; p-
value < 0.0001, two-tailed Student’s t-test), which may contribute to the observed differences in
insulation50.

At promoters, RB and SMC3 localization both occurred at a region ~65 bp upstream of the
transcription start site (TSS) (Fig. 2e). RB-bound promoters were more insulating compared to non-RB-
bound promoters (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 8; p-value = 9.0×10-240, two-tailed Student’s t-test) and
were often co-occupied by E2F1 (Supplementary Fig. 9), leading to decreased nucleosome occupancy at
the TSS and more active transcription (Figs. 2g and h; p-value < 0.0001, two-tailed Student’s t-test).
Notably, the increased insulation at RB-bound promoters was significant when it was compared to non-
RB-bound promoters with similar transcriptional activity (Supplementary Fig. 8; p-value < 0.0001, two-
tailed Student’s t-test).

In brief, we report that RB-bound chromatin loci were also occupied by SMC3 and exhibited
increased insulation. This extensive colocalization of RB and SMC3 on chromatin raises the question of
whether RB-mediated regulation of cohesin-dependent loops results from RB’s direct influence on
cohesin activity, and whether this regulation is confined to RB-bound loci or occurs genome-wide.

RB promotes cohesin removal from CTCF sites across chromosomes
The extensive co-localization of chromatin-bound RB and SMC3, along with the observed impact of
RB loss on cohesin-dependent loop formation and TAD boundary strength, prompted us to investigate
RB’s role in cohesin localization. Upon RB depletion, a clear change in the distribution of SMC3 was
observed genome-wide. Outside DNA repeats, the binding of SMC3 occurred at three distinct types of
cis-regulatory elements: promoters, insulators, and enhancers (Supplementary Fig. 10). In G1-
synchronized cells, RB loss led to an average +14.4% increase (95% confidence interval (CI), 11.1%–
17.7%; n = 4) in the SMC3 signal across 21,498 insulators (Fig. 3a). We reproduced this finding in
biological replicate experiments as well as in different RB1 knockout clones (Fig. 3a). To rule out the
possibility that the observed increase is an indirect effect of RB loss, we compared the proteomes of
RBWT and RBKO cells and found no significant differences in the protein levels of SMC3 or other core
components of the cohesin complex (Supplementary Fig. 11). To exclude the possibility that the observed
changes resulted from normalization artifacts, we utilized spike-in DNA from Escherichia coli as an
additional control and confirmed the increase in SMC3 signal at insulators (Fig. 3a). Notably, we did not
observe analogous increases in SMC3 signal at promoters (+2.8% upon RB loss; n = 4) or enhancers (-
3.4% upon RB loss; n = 4), further supporting the specificity of RB’s regulatory role at insulator sites.
Notably, the enrichment of signal at insulators occurred across the chromosome and was not confined to
RB-bound loci (Supplementary Fig. 10), suggesting that the observed functional interplay between RB
and SMC3 might be distinct from the physical interaction.

To further characterize the functional interplay between RB and SMC3, we performed SMC3 ChIP-seq
experiments in RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells synchronized at different phases of the cell cycle: G1,
S, and prometaphase (Fig. 3b). Synchronization in prometaphase was achieved via nocodazole treatment.
As expected, prometaphase-synchronized cells exhibited weakest SMC3 binding at CTCF insulators,
reflecting the prophase pathway, whereby chromatin-bound cohesin is released from chromosome arms
through a Wapl-dependent mechanism51,52. We also reproduced the reduction in cohesin enrichment at
CTCF insulators upon G1/S transition, thought to result from the dissolution of CTCF-chromatin
interactions by the DNA replication machinery53. Importantly, we identified that RB loss significantly
disturbs cohesin release in prometaphase cells, leading to an average +57.6% increase (95% CI, 42.1%–
73.2%; n = 2) in the SMC3 signal across 21,498 insulators (Fig. 3b). This change was specific (p-value =
1.26×10-3, one-way ANOVA) to insulators and was less pronounced in promoters (+12.2% upon RB loss;
n = 2) and enhancers (+8.2% upon RB loss; n = 2). SMC3 ChIP-seq in RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1
cells synchronized in prometaphase using inhibition of Eg5 kinesin activity, as an alternative to
nocodazole-induced arrest, similarly revealed cohesin enrichment at insulators following RB loss
(Supplementary Fig. 12).

We observed that the RB-mediated deregulation of cohesin distribution peaked during mitosis and
persisted into early G1 (Fig. 3b). Supporting this model, we found that the fold change in SMC3 binding
upon RB depletion was positively correlated between G1 and prometaphase cells, while S-phase cells
showed little to no correlation with either (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 10). Notably, a higher
correlation was observed in regions that gained SMC3 upon RB loss, compared to regions that lost
SMC3. Since RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells synchronized in prometaphase exhibited a dramatic increase in
SMC3 binding at insulators, we wondered which sites lost SMC3 during this process. Therefore, we
performed a DNA motif analysis on regions that gained or lost SMC3 signal upon RB loss (Fig. 3d). We
observed that regions that gained SMC3 were highly enriched with CTCF and BORIS binding motifs,
corroborating our findings that SMC3 gain primarily occurs at insulators. Notably, in regions that lost
SMC3, we did not observe DNA motif enrichment at a similar level to those that gained SMC3 (Fig. 3d).
While AP-1 binding motifs showed statistical significance, AP-1-bound enhancers exhibited an overall
increase in SMC3 signal upon RB loss (Supplementary Fig. 13), and only the strongest AP-1-bound
enhancers (n = 3,652) showed slight reductions in SMC3 signal (-2.3% change upon RB loss). Due to the
relatively small number of these sites and the minimal differences in SMC3 signal, we conclude that AP-
1-bound enhancers are not the primary source of SMC3 loss.

We then assessed repetitive DNA sequences, where a significant fraction of cohesin may localize
(Supplementary Fig. 14)54. As RBWT hTERT-RPE1 cells entered prometaphase, we observed a specific
3.5-fold increase in SMC3 ChIP-seq reads at centromeric α-satellites, with 2.8% of all reads in
prometaphase cells arising from these regions. However, RB loss led to an increased SMC3 binding
(+10.6% upon RB loss) at centromeric α-satellites in prometaphase cells, ruling out the possibility that the
repetitive DNA sequences are the primary source of SMC3 loss upon RB depletion.

Cohesin-dependent loop extrusion is a dynamic process, with the vast majority of cohesin being
partially extruded and not statically localized to TAD boundaries (Fig. 3e)28,30. We therefore hypothesized
that partially extruded cohesin might be the source of SMC3 loss upon RB depletion. Supporting this
hypothesis, in a pooled analysis, we observed a chromosome-wide decrease in SMC3 signal at
intermediary non-SMC3 sites upon RB loss (Fig. 3f). These changes were specific to G1 and
prometaphase cells and not to cells synchronized in S phase. Sequencing of the input DNA showed no
differences in the same regions, confirming that the observed changes in SMC3 signal at intermediary
non-SMC3 sites upon RB loss were not due to differential sequencing coverage (Supplementary Fig. 15).
Overall, we conclude that RB loss perturbs cohesin release in prometaphase, leading to cohesin
enrichment at CTCF insulators and cohesin depletion at intermediary non-SMC3 sites, with these effects
persisting into G1.

RB reduces insulation at TAD boundaries
While RB-mediated changes in SMC3 distribution peaks during the mitosis, these cells typically lack
nuclear compartments and TADs46. Notably, we observed that this deregulation of SMC3 distribution
persists into the G1 phase. This led us to investigate whether RB-mediated changes in SMC3 distribution
affect chromatin organization in G1. A strong negative correlation was found between the difference in
SMC3 ChIP-seq signal and the change in the insulation score (Spearman’s ρ = -0.87, p-value = 1.17×10-
3), suggesting that regions that gained SMC3 following RB loss showed increased insulation (Fig. 3g).
Further analysis of insulation changes at the entire SMC3-bound or RB-bound genomic loci revealed that
RB depletion specifically induced insulation at CTCF-bound insulators and TAD boundaries, while
having the opposite effect in promoters and enhancers (Supplementary Fig. 15).

These changes in insulation were also evident from the differential analysis of chromosome
conformation capture. Reflecting the overall increase in the number of loops upon RB loss, we observed a
4.7-fold increase in the number of loops specific to RBKO compared to RBWT (Supplementary Fig. 16).
Inspection of individual regions in chromosomes 9 and 11 revealed visually striking gains in chromatin
contacts and showed that the formation of differential loops in RBKO is driven by an increase in cohesin
signal at insulators, including SMC3 and STAG1 (Figs. 3h and i). Additional SMC3 ChIP-quantitative
PCR further confirmed the increase of SMC3 binding at chromosome 9 locus following RB loss
(Supplementary Fig. 17). Replicate experiments, using spike-in DNA from Escherichia coli as an
additional control, corroborated the increased SMC3 binding at these insulators upon RB loss.

RB enhances the non-E2F transcriptional program
Insulators are cis-regulatory elements that act as barriers for enhancer-promoter interactions55.
Therefore, we wondered whether the observed interplay between RB and SMC3 at insulators has
implications for enhancer-promoter interactions. To quantify enhancer-promoter interactions, we utilized
H3K27ac HiChIP in RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells synchronized in G136.

Upon RB loss, we observed a general loss of contacts between sites marked by H3K27ac (Figs. 4a–c).
The number of H3K27ac HiChIP peaks decreased 3.3-fold (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 18), and the
average strength of HiChIP interactions was weakened in both biological replicate experiments (Fig. 4b).
Using ChIP-seq tracks for histone modifications, we further categorized these interactions as enhancer-
enhancer, enhancer-promoter, and promoter-promoter interactions (Methods). Among the H3K27ac
HiChIP peaks shared between RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells, 83.3% represented enhancer-enhancer
interactions, 12.0% were enhancer-promoter interactions, and 4.8% were promoter-promoter interactions.
Although RB1 knockout cells display slightly increased H3K27ac ChIP-seq signal compared to RB1 wild-
type hTERT-RPE1 cells, consistent with transcriptional de-repression23, RB depletion reduced the
strength of H3K27ac HiChIP peaks across all three interaction groups (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig.
15). As an orthogonal approach, we performed MED15 ChIP-seq to assess mediator recruitment and
observed reduced MED15 occupancy at enhancers and promoters following RB loss (Fig. 4d and
Supplementary Fig. 19). To further investigate whether the role of RB in regulating enhancer-promoter
interactions associated with its activity in repressing insulation at TAD boundaries, we compared
interactions between enhancer-promoter pairs that cross a TAD boundary (inter-TAD) with those that do
not (intra-TAD). To control distance-dependent effects, we selected a subset of enhancer-promoter pairs
matched for distance (Supplementary Fig. 20). As expected, intra-TAD enhancer-promoter interactions
were stronger and more well-defined, while inter-TAD interactions were weaker and less distinct in both
RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells (Supplementary Fig. 20). Comparing RBWT and RBKO cells revealed
that both intra- and inter-TAD interactions weaken upon RB loss, with the RB-dependent effect appearing
more pronounced when the enhancer-promoter pair spans a TAD boundary. Consistent with this, MED15
ChIP-seq analysis demonstrated that in RBWT cells, TAD boundaries impose a distance-dependent effect
on MED15 ChIP-seq signal and enhancer activity, whereas this pattern is lost in RBKO cells
(Supplementary Figs. 20c and d). Together, these findings suggest that RB-mediated repression of
insulation at TAD boundaries facilitates increased enhancer-promoter interactions in the presence of wild-
type RB, although additional mechanisms may also contribute. Motif enrichment analysis of enhancers
with decreased MED15 binding upon RB loss revealed enrichment of AP-1 and TEAD transcription
factors motifs (Supplementary Fig. 19). Given that RB has been reported to associate with these enhancer
regions23,56, these results raise the possibility that RB regulates enhancer activity through additional
mechanistically distinct pathways.

To assess the transcriptional impact of the RB-mediated changes in H3K27ac interactions, we
compiled a set of 2,656 genes with insulators located between active enhancers and an active promoter
(Fig. 5a). From this set, we identified 1,754 genes that showed no RB or E2F1 binding at the promoter.
We reasoned that this gene set would be ideal for assessing the transcriptional effects of the RB-induced
chromatin rearrangements, as potential complications from RB-mediated repression of E2F activity would
be minimal. Within this gene set, 181 genes showed increased SMC3 binding at the insulator (cohesin
gain), and 44 genes showed decreased SMC3 binding at the insulator (cohesin loss) across experiments,
consistent with the overall increase in SMC3 binding at insulators upon RB loss (Fig. 5b). Although RB
depletion elevates the average expression levels of genes in both RB/E2F-bound and non-RB/non-E2F-
bound promoters (Fig. 5b, left panel), the expression of genes within the ‘cohesin gain’ gene set was
significantly lower compared to the average expression level of genes with non-RB/non-E2F-bound
promoters (Fig. 5b; p-value = 0.0368, two-tailed Student’s t-test) or compared to the ‘cohesin loss’ gene
set (Fig. 5b; p-value = 9.16×10-4, two-tailed Student’s t-test). This indicates that cohesin release at
insulators facilitated by RB impacts transcription and that RB acts via this mechanism to safeguard and
enhance the expression of multiple non-E2F target genes. As an example, we demonstrate RB’s role in
enhancing the expression of lysyl oxidase-like 1 (LOXL1) that correlates with reduced cohesin binding at
an insulator site located between LOXL1 promoter and enhancer (Supplementary Fig. 21).

Gene set enrichment and gene ontology analyses of the 181 genes regulated by cohesin gain at an
adjacent insulator revealed that RB-mediated dysregulation of SMC3 distribution primarily affects genes
regulating epithelial-mesenchymal transition by maintaining epithelial characteristics (Fig. 5c and
Supplementary Fig. 22; p-value = 4.84×10-4, gene set enrichment analysis), and more specifically
extracellular matrix organization (Fig. 5c; p-value = 1.41×10-3, gene ontology: biological processes).
Consistent with these results, we also observed an increased cellular detachment rate in both RBKO clones
assessed compared to RBWT in hTERT-RPE1 cells (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 23; p-value < 0.0001,
two-tailed Student’s t-test). Consistent with this, wound healing assays revealed an elevated migration
rate in RBKO cells compared to RBWT cells (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 24). We also observed
enrichment of genes associated with myogenesis (Fig. 5c; p-value = 1.27×10-2, gene set enrichment
analysis), intriguing in light of previous suggestions that RB behaves as a transcriptional activator during
this process57-59. While these phenotypes do not represent comprehensive functional validation of RB-
regulated chromatin architecture, these cell cycle-independent effects of RB may be a good starting point
for connecting architectural chromatin changes to cellular behavior of RB-deficient cells.

To place these transcriptional changes in context, we clustered the RB-deregulated genes based on the
transcriptional patterns observed in synchronized populations of RBWT and RBKO cells. We identified five
major categories of RB-mediated transcriptional regulation (Fig. 5f). Cluster 3 represents RB-bound
genes suppressed by RB in G1, with promoters enriched in E2F binding motifs (Supplementary Fig. 25).
Cluster 1 includes cell cycle-dependent genes suppressed in G1 in both RBWT and RBKO cells, whose
promoters are enriched in the CHR motif, indicating late cell cycle genes controlled by DREAM and
MMB-FOXM160. The other three groups of the RB-deregulated genes show less RB binding, and their
transcriptional regulation doesn’t follow the canonical RB/E2F model. Of these, cluster 5, a group of G1-
specific genes whose expression is enhanced by RB, exhibited the strongest association with the ‘cohesin
gain’ gene set: 54.5% of differentially expressed genes in this gene set belonged to cluster 5 (Fig. 5f; p-
value = 5.35×10-3, Fisher’s exact test). Notably, the gene set enrichment and gene ontology analyses for
cluster 5 genes revealed similar signatures compared to the ‘cohesin gain’ gene set (Supplementary Fig.
26). Overall, our data indicate that rather than targeting random genes, this previously unrecognized RB
function may regulate specific biological processes. To further investigate whether these RB-associated
transcriptional changes occur population-wide or are driven by a specific cell population, we performed
single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) experiments in RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells synchronized in
the G1 phase via contact inhibition. Principal component analysis revealed that all cells clustered
together, with a modest separation between RBWT and RBKO cells, primarily driven, as expected, by
differences in RB/E2F target gene expression – cluster 3 (Supplementary Fig. 26). Notably, the scRNA-
seq analysis validated the differential expression of cluster 5 genes, where RB functions as a
transcriptional activator during G1 (Supplementary Figs. 27 and 28). While the scRNA-seq experiment
corroborated non-canonical transcriptional activation by RB, it did not reveal additional distinct
transcriptional profiles at the single-cell level that would support RB’s effect on cellular heterogeneity.

## Methods

Cell culture
All cells were cultured at 37ºC with 5% CO2. Non-transformed human retinal pigment
epithelial cells immortalized by human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT-RPE1) were a
gift from Dr. David Pellman’s laboratory (Dana Farber Cancer Institute, RRID: CVCL_4388).
Human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293T) were obtained from ATCC (Cat. # CRL-3216,
RRID: CVCL_0063). hTERT-RPE1 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s
Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 25 mM glucose, 2 mM glutamine, 5% fetal bovine serum,
and antibiotics (penicillin, 100 units/mL; streptomycin, 100 μg/mL). HEK293T cells were
cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 25 mM glucose,
2 mM glutamine, 10% fetal bovine serum, and antibiotics (penicillin, 100 units/mL;
streptomycin, 100 μg/mL). RB1 knockdown or the replacement of endogenous RB with the
constitutively active RB (i.e., RB∆CDK) were done in cells transduced with pINDUCER11
(Addgene, Cat. # 44363) or pINDUCER20 (Addgene, Cat. # 44012) constructs as previously
described14,16. Doxycycline induction was performed by treating cells with doxycycline (Sigma-
Aldrich, Cat. # D9891) at 0.5 μg/mL concentration for 48 h. G1 synchronization was performed
via contact inhibition through maintaining cells for 6 d in a confluent state. Cells were
subsequently released to S phase via trypsinization. For mitotic synchronization in
prometaphase, cells were synchronized to G1 by contact inhibition through maintaining cells in a
confluent state for 6 days. Cells were subsequently released to S phase by trypsinization and
were transferred to T175 (large) flasks to sub-confluent state. After 16 h, cells were treated with
0.1 µg/mL nocodazole (Cell signaling, Cat. #2190) for 6 h or with 5 µM kinesin Eg5 inhibitor
(Eg5i) S-Trityl-L-Cysteine (PMID: 16507573) (Tocris, Cat. #2191) for 24 h. Mitotic cells were
collected by gentle shaking and tapping of the flask. RB1 knockout cell lines were generated by
CRISPR/Cas9 and were previously described21.

Transfections
pINDUCER11 (Addgene, Cat. # 44363, RRID: Addgene_44363), pINDUCER20
(Addgene, Cat. # 44012, RRID: Addgene_44012), pLenti-CMVtight-Puro-DEST (Addgene, Cat.
# 26430, RRID: Addgene_26430), and pLenti-CMVtight-eGFP-Puro (Addgene, Cat. # 26431,
RRID: Addgene_26431) constructs were packaged in HEK293T cells by transient transfection.
Envelope plasmid pCMV-VSV-G (Addgene, Cat. # 8454, RRID: Addgene_8454) and packaging
plasmid pCMV-dR8.2 dvpr (Addgene, Cat. # 8455, RRID: Addgene_8455) were utilized for
transient transfection. Transfections were carried out using X-tremeGENE 9 DNA Transfection
Reagent (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. # 6365787001). All cell lines were infected with lentiviral
particles in the presence of 5 μg/ml polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. # 107689). Stable cell lines
were selected for expression of the green fluorescence protein by fluorescence-activated cell
sorting or for resistance to specific antibiotics: pINDUCER20, 400μg/ml G-418 (Gibco, Cat. #
10131035); and pLenti-CMVtight-Puro-DEST, 6 μg/ml puromycin (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. #
P9620).

Cell cycle analysis
The cell cycle was analyzed for hTERT-RPE1 cells in various conditions. Cells were
incubated with 20 μM 5-ethynyl-2’-deoxyuridine (EdU; Life technologies, Cat. # A10044) for 2
h, fixed with 3.7% formaldehyde in PBS for 15 min, blocked with 3% BSA in PBS for 1 min,
permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 30 min, and stained with ClickIT reaction
(100mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 3mM CuSO4, 50 mM Ascorbic Acid, and 2.5 μM Alexa Fluor-647
azide; Life Technologies, Cat. # A10277) for 30 minutes and 3 μM 4',6-Diamidino-2-
Phenylindole Dihydrochloride (DAPI; Life Technologies, Cat. # D1306) in staining buffer
(100mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2, 0.5 mM MgCl2, and 0.1% NP-40) for
15 minutes. Flow cytometry experiments were performed with LSR II flow cytometer (BD
Biosciences) and were analyzed using the FCS Express software (v7.18.0025).

Heterochromatin dispersion analysis
Coverslips with adhered hTERT-RPE1 cells were washed with PBS and fixed by
sequentially incubating in 70, 85, and 100% ethanol for 2 min each. Coverslips were dried, and
probe mix containing FISH probe for chromosome 7 α-satellite (Cytocell, Cat. # LPE007G) and
hybridization buffer B (Cytocell, Cat. # H1000L) was added. Coverslips were affixed to slides
and sealed using rubber cement. Slides were denatured at 75°C and incubated at 37°C for 16 h.
Coverslips were removed and washed in 0.25× SSC at 72°C and 2× SSC (with 0.05% Tween-20)
for 2 min each. Coverslips were mounted using Vectashield (with DAPI) and sealed. A Zeiss
LSM 710 Laser Scanning Confocal Microscope and Zeiss ZEN software were used to acquire
FISH images. Images were captured using parameters for each probe that remained consistent
across samples and experiments. Images were acquired at room temperature, and a Plan-
Apochromat 63×/1.40 Oil DIC M27 (Zeiss, Cat. # 420782-9900-000) was used to capture Z-
stacks (6–12 sections of 0.5-µM thickness). FITC/Alexa Fluor 488 filter was used to acquire
images for chromosome 7 α-satellite. Maximum projections of Z-stacks were used for image
analysis. No other image processing was performed. Images were analyzed using Fiji (ImageJ)
software. To effectively quantify the dispersion phenotype, we used a skeleton dot length plugin,
and macros were made to execute the steps as previously described (14). The following macro
steps were written and executed in FIJI: open();setOption(“BlackBackground”, false);
run(“Make Binary”); run(“Dilate”); run(“Dilate”); run(“Dilate”); run(“Skeletonize”);
run(“Analyze Skeleton (2D/3D)”, “prune=none calculate show display”). Cutoffs of skeleton dot
length were used to define the foci categories as compact, diffused, and dispersed: compact,
<0.75 µm; diffused, 0.75–1.25 µm; and dispersed, >1.25 µm.

Cell detachment rate analysis
For the cell detachment experiment, hTERT-RPE1 cells were seeded on 24-well plates and
synchronized to G1 in confluent culture for 6 days. Cells were collected after treatment with
0.25% trypsin (Corning, Cat. # 25-053-CI) for 1 to 6 minutes, and the number of cells was
assessed using the TC20 automated cell counter (Bio-Rad). Brightfield images of the cells that
remained attached on the plate surface after trypsinization were obtained using the Diaphot 300
inverted microscope (Nikon), 4x objective lens.

Wound healing assay
hTERT-RPE1 cells were seeded on 6-well plates and synchronized to G1 in confluent
culture for 6 days. On the sixth day of contact inhibition, wounds were generated in a straight
line using a 1 mm pipette tip. After scratch, the cell monolayer was washed with PBS to remove
detached cells and replenished with fresh reduced DMEM media supplemented with 25 mM
glucose, 2 mM glutamine, antibiotics (i.e., penicillin, 100 units/mL; streptomycin, 100 μg/mL)
and 1% fetal bovine serum. Serum starvation at 1% fetal bovine serum was performed to prevent
cells from proliferating, and its concentration was determined by assessing the minimum
concentration of serum that prevents cells from dying. At 0.5% and 0.05% fetal bovine serum,
we observed that most cells died due to the lack of sufficient serum. The images were acquired
immediately following media replacement (t = 0 hours) and after 2 days (t = 48 hours) using an
inverted microscope (Nikon, Diaphot 300), 4x objective lens. A Bandpass filter was applied to
the images (Process > FFT > Bandpass Filter Image, large structure equal to 40 pixels, small
structure equal to 3.0 pixels, tolerance = 5%).

Wound healing image analysis
Wound areas were assessed using ImageJ (v1.54d). Briefly, images were first converted to
8-bit (Image > Type > 8-bit) and the threshold was reset (Image > Adjust > Threshold > Reset).
A Bandpass filter was applied to the images (Process > FFT > Bandpass Filter Image, large
structure equal to 40 pixels, small structure equal to 3.0 pixels, tolerance= 5%) and the threshold
was adjusted to 85% (Image > Adjust > Threshold). An additional filter of minimum radius
equal to 5.0 pixels was used (Process > Filters > Minimum > Radius). The area was selected
using the wand tool and measured in pixels (Analyze > Measure).

Micro-C
Micro-C experiments were performed using the Micro-C kit (10X wash buffer, NWB
solution, chromatin capture beads, streptavidin beads, 20% SDS, crosslink reversal buffer,
MNase enzyme mix, 10X nuclease digest buffer, 100 mM MgCl2, 0.5 M EGTA, end polishing
buffer, end polishing enzyme mix, intra-aggregate ligation buffer, intra-aggregate ligation
enzyme mix, bridge, 5X bridge ligation buffer, bridge ligase, proteinase K, 250 mM DTT, and
HotStart PCR Ready Mix; Dovetail Genomics, Cat. # 21006) via Dovetail Genomics’ Micro-C
service (Cat. # 20020). In short, frozen hTERT-RPE1 cells were resuspended in 1X PBS,
crosslinked with crosslinked using 3 mM disuccinimidyl glutarate (DSG; Thermo Fisher
Scientific, Cat. # A35392) and 1% formaldehyde. MNase reaction was performed using 0.5 μL
of MNase enzyme mix in a 100 μL solution of 1X nuclease digest buffer and was stopped by
addition of 5 μL of 0.5 M EGTA. Digested chromatin was solubilized by supplementing with 3
μL of 20% SDS and was captured by chromatin capture beads. End polishing was performed
using the end polishing enzyme mix at the end polishing buffer, and crosslinks were reversed by
1X crosslink reversal buffer supplemented with proteinase K. DNA was purified using
SPRIselect beads (Beckman Coulter, Cat. # B23317). The sequencing library was prepared using
the Dovetail Library Module for Illumina (end repair enzyme mix, end repair enzyme buffer,
ligation enhancer, ligation enzyme mix, adaptor for Illumina, and USER enzyme mix; Dovetail
Genomics, Cat. # DG-LIB-001). End repair enzyme mix and end repair buffer supplemented
with 12 mM DTT were utilized for end repair, which were followed by adapter ligation and
USER digest. 2.5 μL adaptor for Illumina, 30 μL ligation enzyme mix, and 1 μL ligation
enhancer were used for the 33.5 μL reaction mixture. DNA was then purified with SPRIselect
beads (Beckman Coulter, Cat. # B23317), ligation captured via streptavidin beads, and
underwent Index PCR using the HotStart PCR ready mix. Size selection was performed using
SPRIselect beads (Beckman Coulter, Cat. # B23317). The final libraries were run on the
NovaSeq 6000 system (Illumina) in technical quadruplicates on a paired-end mode. On average,
1.3 billion reads were sequenced per sample to achieve nucleosome resolution.

Bioinformatics processing for Micro-C
Library quality control was performed on the first 2 million reads via the get_gc.py code
provided by Dovetail Genomics (https://github.com/dovetail-genomics/Micro-C). Sequencing
reads were aligned to the hg38 human reference build using bwa mem (v0.7.17-r1198-dirty).
Pairtools (v0.3.0) were utilized to parse, sort, and deduplicate ligation sequencing reads to valid
pairs. On average, 80.0% of sequencing reads were mapped as valid pairs, 13.3% were single-
sided, and 6.5% were unmapped. Juicer Tools pre (v1.22.0) was utilized to generate .hic files for
the chromosome conformation capture maps at 5 kb resolution. JuiceBox (v1.11.08) was utilized
to visualize chromosome conformation capture maps in the .hic format. For .hic files, the
aggregate peak analysis was performed using the APA (v1.22.0) algorithm. Most of the
subsequent analyses were performed after converting the .hic files to .cool and .mcool formats
using hic2cool (v0.5.1) at 10 kb resolution. The .cool files were matrix balanced using cooler
balance (v0.9.2). For analyses that does not require full resolution, .cool files were coarsened
using cooler coarsen (v0.9.2) to 1 Mb resolution and was matrix balanced using cooler balance
(v0.9.2). Expected number of cis contacts were quantified using the cooltools expected_cis
function (v0.5.2) and were utilized for log observed/expected visualization. The visualization of
.cool files were performed using cooltools pileup (v0.5.2) and coolpup.py (v1.0.0). For the
visualization of chromosome conformation capture map simultaneously with other sequencing
tracks, we utilized pyGenomeTracks (v3.8). The .hic files were converted to .h5 format using
HiCExplorer hicConvertFormat (v2.2.1.1) for usage. Normalization methods utilized in this
study were as follows: .hic files, Knight-Ruiz matrix balancing; .cool and .mcool files, iterative
correction and eigenvector decomposition (ICE); and .h5 files, Knight-Ruiz matrix balancing.

Contact probability
Contact probability, also known as P(s) (22, 24), was measured using cooltools (v0.5.2) at
10 kb resolution. Smoothed aggregate curve was produced using cooltools expected_cis (v0.5.2)
and its first derivative was assessed using NumPy gradient (v1.22.3). The visualization of the
curves was performed using loglog and semilogx functions of Matplotlib (v3.4.2).

Nuclear compartment analysis
The visualization of Pearson correlation map was performed using JuiceBox (v1.11.08).
Nuclear compartment analysis was performed by quantifying the eigenvector of the chromosome
conformation capture matrix using cooltools eigs_cis (v0.5.2). Eigenvector tracks were then
exported to bigWig via Bioframe to_bigwig (v0.3.3). The assignment of compartments A/B was
performed by comparing the eigenvector track to the ATAC-seq data for hTERT-RPE1 cell lines
generated in this study. Saddle plots, generated from cooltools saddle (v0.5.2), were utilized to
assess the distribution of compartments and interactions between compartments.

Quantification of insulation score
The insulation score (30-33) was measured from .mcool files using cooltools insulation
(v0.5.2) at 10 kb resolution using four different window sizes: 30 kb, 50 kb, 100 kb, and 250 kb.
For subsequent analyses, insulation scores measured from the window size of 100 kb were
utilized. Insulation scores were then filtered for good bins via the “is_bad_bin” column of the
insulation table and were subsequently exported to bigWig via Bioframe to_bigwig (v0.3.3). The
assessment of average insulation score at a region was assessed by deeptools
multiBigwigSummary (v3.5.1).

Analyses of cohesin-dependent loops, topologically associating domains, and architectural
stripes
The HiCCUPS algorithm (v1.22.0) was utilized to identify chromatin loops from
chromosome conformation capture maps, and the HiCCUPS Diff algorithm (v1.22.0) was
utilized to identify differential loop formation in G1-synchronized RBWT and RBKO hTERT-
RPE1 cells. For the assessment of topologically associating domains, the insulation table
acquired from .mcool files through cooltools insulation (v0.5.2) was utilized. From the insulation
table, good bins and strong boundaries were filtered by “is_bad_bin” and “is_boundary_100kb”
columns, respectively, and were utilized as topologically associating domain boundaries. For
visualization, topologically associating domains with sizes from 300 kb to 400 kb were
aggregated using cooltools (v0.5.2). The architectural stripes were identified by the Stripenn
algorithm (v1.1.65.15) on .mcool files at 10 kb resolution with default parameters.

3D reconstruction of nuclear organization
3D reconstruction of nuclear organization from chromosome conformation capture maps
were performed using the PGS algorithm (v0.0.1). The topologically associating domains from
cooltools insulation (v0.5.2) were utilized, and the PGS algorithm simulated 100 structures at a 1
Mb resolution. The following values of theta were utilized for modeling: 1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02,
and 0.01. The nucleus radius were simulated as 5 μm, and the average location of each
topologically associating domain beads were assessed by taking the average of 100 structures
that were generated. For visualization, .pqr files were generated using the PGS hms_to_pdb.py
(v0.0.1) function, and a PyMOL (v2.5.2) code for each file was generated to alter the radius of
each topologically associating domain beads. Mesh visualization was used to create figures, and
the structures were ray traced using POV-Ray (v3.7.0.msvc10).

HiChIP
The HiChIP MNase library was prepared using the Dovetail HiChIP MNase Kit for
mammalian cells (Cat. # 21007), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, 5×106 frozen
hTERT-RPE1 cells were used and chromatin was crosslinked with 0.3 M disuccinimidyl
glutarate (DSG; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. # A35392) and 1% formaldehyde (Sigma-
Aldrich, Cat. # F8775). The cross-linked chromatin was digested in situ with micrococcal
nuclease. The MNase reaction was performed using 0.5 μL of MNase enzyme mix in a 100 μL
solution of 1X nuclease digest buffer and was stopped by addition of 10 μL of 0.5 M EGTA
(Dovetail Mico-C Module Box 2, Cat. # DG-NUC-001). The cross-linked, digested chromatin
was then extracted upon cell lysis with 1X RIPA and solubilized with 1 μL of 20% SDS
(Dovetail Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Core Box 1, Cat. # DG-NUC-001). Chromatin
fragments from 1000 ng of lysates were incubated with 300 ng of antibody against H3K27ac
(Cell Signaling, Cat. # 8173) overnight for chromatin immunoprecipitation. The antibody-
protein-DNA complex was pulled down with protein A/G-coated beads (Dovetail Chromatin
Immunoprecipitation Core Box 1, Cat. # DG-NUC-001). Next, the chromatin ends were repaired
and ligated to a biotinylated bridge adapter followed by proximity ligation of adapter-containing
ends as described by the manufacturer (Dovetail Mico-C Module Box 2, Cat. # DG-NUC-001).
After proximity ligation, the crosslinks were reversed, and the associated proteins were degraded
by 1X crosslink reversal buffer supplemented with proteinase K (Dovetail Chromatin
Immunoprecipitation Core Box 1 and Dovetail Mico-C Module Box 2, Cat. # DG-NUC-001).
DNA was purified using SPRI select beads (Beckman Coulter, Cat. # B23317), and then
converted into a sequencing library using Illumina-compatible adaptors (Dovetail Dual Index
Primer Set #1 for Illumina, Cat. # DG-PRS-002 and Dovetail Library Module for Illumina, Cat.
# DG-LIB-001). Biotin-containing fragments were isolated using streptavidin beads prior to PCR
amplification (Dovetail Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Core Box 1 and Dovetail Mico-C
Module Box 2, Cat. # DG-NUC-001). Size selection was performed using SPRIselect beads
(Beckman Coulter, Cat. # B23317). The libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq 6000
(Illumina) platform to generate 300 million read pairs with length of 150 bp.

Bioinformatics processing for HiChIP
Adapter trimming was performed using trim-galore in a paired-end mode to remove
Illumina adapter sequences. Sequencing reads were aligned to the hg38 human reference build
using bwa mem (v0.7.17-r1188). Pairtools (v0.3.0) were utilized to parse, sort, and deduplicate
ligation sequencing reads to valid pairs. Juicer Tools pre (v1.22.01) was utilized to generate .hic
files for the chromosome conformation capture maps. JuiceBox (v1.11.08) was utilized to
visualize chromosome conformation capture maps in the .hic format. For .hic files, the aggregate
peak analysis was performed using the APA (v1.22.01) algorithm. Most of the subsequent
analyses were performed after converting the .hic files to .cool and .mcool formats using
hic2cool (v0.5.1) at 100 kb resolution. The .cool files were matrix balanced using cooler balance
(v0.9.2). Expected number of cis contacts were quantified using the cooltools expected_cis
function (v0.5.2) and were utilized for log observed/expected visualization. The visualization of
.cool files were performed using cooltools pileup (v0.5.2) and coolpup.py (v1.0.0). For the
visualization of chromosome conformation capture map simultaneously with other sequencing
tracks, we utilized pyGenomeTracks (v3.8). The .hic files were converted to .h5 format using
HiCExplorer hicConvertFormat (v2.2.1.1) for usage. Normalization methods utilized in this
study were as follows: .hic files, Knight-Ruiz matrix balancing; .cool and .mcool files, iterative
correction and eigenvector decomposition (ICE); and .h5 files, Knight-Ruiz matrix balancing.
H3K27ac HiChIP peaks were called using FitHiChIP (v11.0) using valid pairs. The peak file for
H3K27ac ChIP-seq was prepared using MACS (v2.2.7.1) using default parameters. The
following parameters for FitHiChIP were utilized: BINSIZE, 100 kb; LowDistThr, 200 kb;
UppDistThr, 10 Mb; UseP2PBackgrnd, 0; BiasType, 1; MergeInt, 1; and QVALUE, 0.01. To
assign each H3K27ac HiChIP peaks as enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter, and promoter-
promoter interactions, we assessed ATAC-seq peaks and ChIP-seq peaks for H3K4me3,
H3K4me1, H3K27ac, and H3K27me3 modifications and identified enhancers and promoters for
each bin. For each H3K27ac HiChIP peak, we measured the number of enhancer-enhancer,
enhancer-promoter, and promoter-promoter pairs, and we assessed the maximum number of
pairs using a custom MATLAB (vR2023a) code. The code is available at our GitHub repository
(https://github.com/hanjunlee21/Lee-et-al-2023).

ChIP-seq
ChIP assays were carried out on hTERT-RPE1 cell cultures using approximately 5 million
cells per sample and per epitope. Cells were washed once with PBS and fixed with 1.5 mM
ethylene glycol bis(succinimidyl succinate) (Thermo Scientific, Cat. # 21565) for 30 min at 25ºC
and 1% formaldehyde (Sigma, Cat. # F8775) for 10 min at 37ºC. 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and
150 mM glycine were used to quench cross-linking. Cell pellets were washed twice with ice-cold
PBS, and lysates were prepared using 300 μL lysis buffer (50mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 1% SDS,
and 0.25% DOC) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors cocktail (PPI) (Thermo
Scientific, Cat. # 78442) for 10 min on ice. Cell lysates were diluted with 900 μL ChIP dilution
buffer (50mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 0.1% SDS, 150 mM NaCl, and 1.84% Triton-X) supplemented
with PPI. Chromatin was fragmented to a size of 200–700 bases with Branson 250 sonifier.
Solubilized chromatin was further diluted with 1800 μL ChIP dilution buffer and
immunoprecipitated with the indicated antibodies overnight at 4°C. Anti-DYKDDDDK Tag
(Cell Signaling, Cat. # 14793) was used for FLAG-RB ChIP, and for other proteins, their
primary antibodies listed in the Antibodies subheadings were utilized for ChIP. Antibody-
chromatin complexes were pulled down with protein G-Dynabeads (Life Technologies, Cat. #
10004D) for 2 hours at 4°C and washed 3 times with RIPA 150 Wash Buffer (0.1% SDS, 0.1%
DOC 1% Triton X-100, 1 mM EDTA, 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), and 150mM NaCl), 3 times with
RIPA 500 Wash Buffer (0.1% SDS, 0.1% DOC, 1% Triton X-100, 1 mM EDTA, 10 mM Tris-
HCl (pH 8), and 500 mM NaCl), 3 times with LiCl wash buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 250
mM LiCl, 0.5% Triton X-100, and 0.5% DOC) and once with ice-cold 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8).
Chromatin complexes were eluted from the beads using elution buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8),
0.1% SDS, 150 mM NaCl, and 5 mM DTT) for 1 hour at 65°C and were treated with RNase A
(Roche, Cat. # 11119915001) for 30 min at 37°C. Proteinase K (Thermo Scientific, Cat. #
25530049) treatment and reverse cross-linking was performed for 3 hours at 65°C. After reversal
of the crosslinks, immunoprecipitated DNA was extracted with AMP Pure XP beads (Beckman
Coulter, Cat. # A63881). ChIP DNA was quantified with Qubit dsDNA HS Assay kit (Thermo
Scientific, Cat. # Q32851). 1–2 ng ChIP DNA samples were used to prepare sequencing
libraries, using the Ovation Ultralow System IV2 kit (TECAN, Cat. # 0344NB-A01). ChIP DNA
and input controls were sequenced using the NextSeq 500/550 High Output Kit v2.5 (75 Cycles)
(Illumina, Cat. # 20024906) with the NextSeq 500 sequencer (Illumina) or with the NovaSeq
6000 sequencer (Illumina). For spike-in controls, DNA fragments from genomic DNA of TOP10
strain of Escherichia coli (Invitrogen, Cat. # C404010) were added to the samples before library
preparation. 5% of spike-in DNA was added compared to the samples to be sequenced.

ChIP- quantitative PCR
Anti-SMC3 (Abcam, Cat. # ab9263) ChIP assays were carried out on hTERT-RPE1 cell
cultures synchronized in pro-metaphase using approximately 5 million cells per
immunoprecipitation, as described in the ChIP-seq method. 0.1-0.2 ng ChIP DNA samples were
analyzed, along with input DNA, using the Roche LightCycler 480 system, as described before
(PMID: 35019938). ChIP real-time PCR primers that were used; CHR9_SMC3_peak_F: 5’-
GACAGGGAGTTGGGGTATGAAA-3’, CHR9_SMC3_peak_R: 5’-
CATTAAGAACAACGGGGCTGAC-3’, CHR9_non-target_F: 5’-
GGTGCTTGTAAAAGGATGCTTAGAT-3’, CHR9_non-target_R: 5’-
CTGGCAGGAACAGAAACAGGG-3’. Average scores from three technical replicates were
calculated. P-values were calculated with ordinary one-way ANOVA multiple comparisons
using GraphPad Prism8 software.

Bioinformatics processing for ChIP-seq
Adapter trimming was performed using trim-galore in a paired-end mode to remove
Illumina adapter sequences. Sequencing reads were then aligned using bwa mem (v0.7.17-r1188)
either to the hg38 human reference genome build or the chimera build of hg38 human reference
genome build and NZ_CP080620.1 Escherichia coli TOP10 strain reference genome build. After
the aligned .bam file was sorted and indexed using samtools (v1.10), sambamba (v0.7.1) was
utilized to sort, mark duplicate reads, and index .bam files. Then, we filtered reads in the .bam
files to produce a file that only contains reads that are not PCR duplicates, with less than or equal
to two mismatches, and with mapping quality that is greater than or equal to 30. After indexing
the .bam file, deeptools bamCoverage (v3.5.1) was utilized to normalize the number of reads
based on counts per million (CPM), and .bigWig files were generated at a 1 bp resolution. Peak
calling was performed as previously described (15), using bedGraph2Cluster with the following
parameters: fold change, 2; normalization, QNorm; distance method, sqeuclidean; and clustering
method, symmetry-collapsed profile and scalar. Alternatively, MACS (v2.2.7.1) was utilized to
call peaks. For samples with spike-in controls, spike-in normalization was performed by
multiplying the data column in each bedGraph file with a scaling factor. The scaling factor was
determined by dividing the number of reads that are aligned to the NZ_CP080620.1 Escherichia
coli TOP10 strain reference genome build by the total number of aligned reads and further
multiplying the value by 1,000,000 and rounding it. For the assessment of repetitive sequences,
sequencing reads were realigned to the hg38 human reference genome build via bowtie
(v2.3.5.1) and were analyzed using RepEnrich (v2) using the Python programming language
(v2.7.18). The fold change upon RB loss was assessed using the read counts calculated from
RBWT and RBKO samples in hTERT-RPE1 cells, and their z-scores were measured. Statistical
significance was measured using the z-score, and the p-values were utilized to generate the
Manhattan plot. For the identification of cohesin gain and cohesin loss gene set, a custom
MATLAB code was utilized. The code is available at our GitHub repository
(https://github.com/hanjunlee21/Lee-et-al-2023). In brief, the list of promoters from Ensembl
(v105) and the list of enhancers from histone modification-based clustering analysis of H3K27ac
ChIP-seq peaks were assessed. Promoters that were non-RB-bound and non-E2F1-bound and
those that were within 60 kb from the nearest enhancer were utilized.

Motif analysis
Motif analysis was performed using the HOMER (v4.11.1) algorithm. Absolute motif
analysis was performed using HOMER findMotifsGenome.pl (v4.11.1) without a preset
background and a size parameter given by the peak file. Differential motif analysis was
performed using HOMER fnidMotifsGenome.pl (v4.11.1) using a different peak file as a
background and a size parameter that is given by the peak file.

ATAC-seq
hTERT-RPE1 cells were synchronized to G1 by contact inhibition for 6 days and
subsequently released to S phase via trypsinization. Cells were harvested and counted using an
automated cell counter (Bio-Rad, TC20). The viability of the cells was assessed at 95% of the
total number of cells after staining them with trypan blue (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat.
#15250061). For each reaction, 100,000 cells were collected and washed with PBS. The ATAC-
seq was performed using an ATAC-seq kit (Active Motif, Cat. # 53150) as described by the
manufacturer. Briefly, cells were resuspended in cold lysis buffer provided by the ATAC-seq kit
(Active Motif, Cat. # 53150) and centrifuged at 1000xg for 10 min at 4°C. The nuclei pellet was
resuspended in the tagmentation buffer provided by the ATAC-seq kit (Active Motif Cat. #
53150) and the reaction was incubated at 37°C for 30 min. Tagmented DNA was purified and
used to generate sequencing libraries following the manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were
sequenced to a minimum depth of 25 million paired end reads with an NovaSeq 6000 sequencer
(Illumina).

Bioinformatics processing for ATAC-seq
Adapter trimming was performed using trim-galore in a paired-end mode to remove
Illumina adapter sequences. Sequencing reads were then aligned using bwa mem (v0.7.17-r1188)
to the hg38 human reference genome build. After the aligned .bam file was sorted and indexed
using samtools (v1.10), sambamba (v0.7.1) was utilized to sort, mark duplicate reads, and index
.bam files. Then, we filtered reads in the .bam files to produce a file that only contains reads that
are not PCR duplicates, with less than or equal to two mismatches, and with mapping quality that
is greater than or equal to 30. After indexing the .bam file, deeptools bamCoverage (v3.5.1) was
utilized to normalize the number of reads based on counts per million (CPM), and .bigWig files
were generated at a 1 bp resolution. Peak calling was performed as previously described (15),
using bedGraph2Cluster with the following parameters: fold change, 2; normalization, QNorm;
distance method, sqeuclidean; and clustering method, symmetry-collapsed profile and scalar.
Alternatively, MACS (v2.2.7.1) was utilized to call peaks.

Validation of RB1 mutation
For the validation of RB1 mutations, RBWT and RBKO hTERT-RPE1 cells were harvested
from culture, and approximately 5 million cells per sample were utilized. After the chromatin
was isolated from cells, the chromatin was digested with micrococcal nuclease. 1–2 ng MNase-
digested DNA samples were used to prepare sequencing libraries, using the Ovation Ultralow
System V2 kit (TECAN, Cat. # 0344NB-A01) and were subsequently sequenced using the
NovaSeq 6000 sequencer (Illumina) using the S4 flow cell. Adapter trimming was performed
using trim-galore in a paired-end mode to remove Illumina adapter sequences. Sequencing reads
were then aligned using bwa mem (v0.7.17-r1188) to the hg38 human reference genome build.
After the aligned .bam file was sorted and indexed using samtools (v1.10), sambamba (v0.7.1)
was utilized to sort, mark duplicate reads, and index .bam files. Then, we filtered reads in the
.bam files to produce a file that only contains reads that are not PCR duplicates, with less than or
equal to two mismatches, and with mapping quality that is greater than or equal to 30.

RNA-seq
hTERT-RPE1 cells after 6 d of contact inhibition or trypsinization were used for RNA-seq
experiments. The RNA-seq experiment for each experimental condition was performed in
biological triplicates. Total RNA was extracted from cells using the Direct-zol RNA MiniPrep
Plus kit (Zymo Research, Cat. # R2073). Multiplexed RNA sequencing libraries were prepared
using the TruSeq library prep kit (Illumina, Cat. # RS-122-2301/2), which utilizes Oligo-dT
beads to capture polyA tails. Paired-end 150 bp reads were collected by the NovaSeq 6000
sequencer (Illumina).

Bioinformatics processing for RNA-seq
Adapter trimming was performed using trim-galore in a paired-end mode to remove
Illumina adapter sequences. Sequencing reads were then aligned using STAR (v2.7.1a) to the
hg38 human reference genome build. A two-pass alignment pipeline was utilized, where the first
pass was performed using the sjdbOverhang of 149 and the sjdbGTFfile from Ensembl (v105)
and the second pass was performed using the SJ.out.tab files generated from the first pass
alignment. Separately, STAR-Fusion (v2.7.1a) was utilized to identify gene fusions using the
RNA-seq dataset. The .bam files generated by the STAR aligner were sorted and indexed via
samtools (v1.10) and were subsequently merged via samtools merge (v1.10) to create a single
file per experimental condition. Deeptools bamCoverage (v3.5.1) was then utilized to normalize
the number of reads based on counts per million (CPM), and .bigWig files were generated at a 1
bp resolution. The calculation of the expression level, on the other hand, was performed on
individual replicate experiments using the RSEM (v1.3.1) algorithm in a paired-end mode.
After RSEM calculation, the read count table was exported to R programming language (v4.3.0),
and DESeq2 (v1.40.2) was utilized to assess the differentially expressed genes. k-means clustering of
the RNA-seq expression profiles generated from this pipeline was utilized using a custom
MATLAB algorithm on the transcripts per million values calculated from RSEM (v1.3.1). The
custom code is available at our GitHub repository [https://github.com/hanjunlee21/Lee-et-al-
2023]. In brief, the k-means clustering was performed using a variation of the kmeans function of
MATLAB (vR2023a) and identified five major categories of transcriptional regulation in our
experiments. The gene set enrichment and gene ontology analyses were performed using Enrichr
and were done by providing the gene symbols generated from analyses, including the cohesin
gain and cohesin loss gene sets as well as the five transcriptional regulation categories.

Single-cell RNA-seq
RBWT and RBKO RPE1 cells arrested in G1 phase by 6 days of contact inhibition were
collected for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq). Cells were washed twice with RPMI
containing 10% heat-inactivated FCS, filtered through a 50 μm filter (Sysmex, Cat#04-004-2327),
followed by cell concentration and viability assessment using trypan blue with a Bright-Line
hemocytometer (Cat#1492), with both samples reaching 95% cell viability. Gene expression
libraries were constructed using the 10x Genomics GEM-X Universal 3’ Gene Expression v4
reagent kits (1000691, 1000690, and 1000215) according to the manufacturer's guidelines. Quality
control was assessed for both cDNA and gene-expression libraries using Qubit dsDNA High
Sensitivity Kit (Invitrogen, Cat#Q32854) and the Agilent High Sensitivity Bioanalyzer DNA Kit
(Cat#5067-4626). Both samples were sequenced on a single lane of an Illumina NovaSeq X 25B
flow-cell to yield a total of ~2 billion reads, using the following read configurations: Read 1- 28
cycles; Read 2- 90 cycles, and dual barcodes with 10 cycles each (i7 and i5 primers).

Proteomics
Cell pellets were processed as previously described75. Briefly, cell pellets were lysed in
500 µL of lysis buffer (75 mM NaCl, 3 % SDS, 1 mM NaF, 1 mM beta-glycerophosphate, 1 mM
sodium orthovanadate, 10 mM sodium pyrophosphate, 1 mM PMSF and 1X Roche Complete
Mini EDTA free protease inhibitors in 50 mM EPPS, pH 8.5). Proteins were then reduced with 5
mM DTT at 56C for 30 min and alkylated with 15 mM iodoacetamide in the dark at room
temperature for 20 min. The reaction was stopped by adding DTT (5 mM final concentration)
and incubated in the dark at room temperature for 15 minutes. Proteins were precipitated by
adding one part trichloroacetic acid to four parts protein solution, followed by 10 minutes of
incubation on ice. The precipitated proteins were pelleted by centrifugation (15,000 g, 10 min,
4°C) and washed twice with prechilled acetone (-20°C, 300 µL, 15,000 g, 10 min, 4°C). The
protein pellets were then resuspended in 1M urea in 50mM EPPS, ph8.5 and digested in a two-
step process (overnight digestion at room temperature with 1 µg/µL of Lys-C (Wako) followed
by six hours of digestion with trypsin (sequencing grade, Promega) at a final concentration of 1
ng/μL for 6 hr at 37 ˚C). The digest was acidified with 10 % trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and
peptides were desalted on C18 solid-phase extraction (SPE) (Sep-Pak, Waters) columns. The
concentration of the desalted peptide solutions was measured with a BCA assay, and 25 ug of
peptides were aliquoted. The samples were dried under vacuum, and stored at -80 ˚C. The TMT
labeling was performed with 18-plex tandem mass tag (TMT) reagents (Thermo Scientific) as
previously described75. The 25 µg of peptide aliquotes were resuspended in 25 µL of 200 mM
EPPS (pH 8.5), 30% acetonitrile (ACN). Labeling was performed by adding 70 μg TMT reagent
in anhydrous ACN and incubating at room temperature for 1 h. The reaction was stopped by
addition of 5% (w/v) hydroxylamine in 200 mM EPPS (pH 8.5) to a final concentration of 0.5%
hydroxylamine and incubation at room temperature for 15 min. Samples were acidified with 1%
TFA, and samples were combined. The pooled samples were desalted using Sep- Pak C18 SPE
cartridges and vacuum dried. The multiplexed samples were fractionated using high-performance
liquid chromatography (HPLC) under basic pH, as previously described75, and dried. The dried
peptides were resuspended in 5 % ACN/5 % formic acid and analyzed in 3-hour runs via
reversed phase LC-MS2/MS3 on an Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer using the Simultaneous
Precursor Selection (SPS) supported MS3 method76. MS2 spectra were assigned using a
SEQUEST-based in-house built proteomics analysis platform using a target-decoy database-
based search strategy to assist filtering for a false-discovery rate (FDR) of protein identifications
of less than 1 %77. Peptides that matched to more than one protein were assigned to that protein
containing the largest number of matched redundant peptide sequences following the law of
parsimony. TMT reporter ion intensities were extracted from the MS3 spectra, selecting the most
intense ion within a 0.003-m/z window centered at the predicted m/z value for each reporter ion,
and spectra were used for quantification if the sum of the S/N values of all reporter ions divided
by the number of analyzed channels was ≥10 and the isolation specificity for the precursor ion
was ≥0.75. Protein intensities were calculated by summing the TMT reporter ions for all peptides
assigned to a protein. The full proteome data was normalized in a two-step process, a row
(protein) normalization followed by a column (sample) normalization. The row normalization
involved scaling the row intensity values by the global median of all row means divided by each
rows mean, adjusting each row mean to equal the global median. Similarly, the column
normalization involved scaling the column intensities so that each column median would be
equal the average of all sample medians. The proteome profiles were generated from
quadruplicate RBWT and RBKO RPE1 cell cultures arrested in G1 phase by 6 days of contact
inhibition. The normalized protein intensities were further processed with Perseus software
(Version 1.6.15.0)78. Identified proteins were compared for deregulation (FDR-threshold < 0.15
and log fold change > 0.7 or < 0.7 between samples) and visualized by using VolcaNoseR
package in R-studio.

Statistics & Reproducibility
All statistical analysis was performed using the OriginPro (v2023b) software. For
comparison of one group against a specific value, two-tailed one-sample Student’s t-test was
utilized (Fig. 2c). For comparison of a paired dataset, two-tailed paired Student’s t-test was
utilized (Fig. 1f). Comparisons of two groups were performed using a two-tailed two-sample
Student’s t-test (Figs. 1g, 2c, 2d, 2h, 5b, 5d, and 5e). To assess statistical significance of DNA
motif enrichment, HOMER79 algorithm’s default two-tailed hypergeometric test followed by a
Benjamini-Hochberg multiple hypotheses correction was utilized. Other enrichment analyses
were performed using a two-tailed Fisher’s exact test. No statistical method was used to
predetermine sample size, and no data were excluded from the analyses. The experiment were
not applicable for randomization, while differential analysis algorithms for Micro-C, HiChIP,
ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq experiments were blinded to the conditions. The calculated
statistical significance is indicated as ∗p-value<0.05; ∗∗p-value<0.01; and ∗∗∗p-value<0.001.
